prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks took Katori's magic-wavelength idea, in which the lattice light shifts both clock levels equally so that the atoms can be held without perturbing the transition, and made it into the most accurate measurement devices ever built. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 mean that the gravitational redshift can be seen over millimetres to centimetres, that drifts of fundamental constants and ultralight dark matter can be searched for, and that the second can be redefined. This is a discovery-type result in my own field: theory and experiment agree quantitatively, the systematics (blackbody shifts, hyperfine and higher-order light shifts, collisions) are understood from first-principles atomic structure, and the platform has been reproduced and surpassed in JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and elsewhere, with intercontinental comparisons. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: a two-person prize, with the concept and first Sr lattice clock (Katori) and the extreme-accuracy and many-body-clock realisation (Ye). The achievement is distinct from the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems: those provided the ruler and the single-ion toolkit, whereas the lattice clock is a new way of interrogating many atoms at once.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier metrology prizes. Ye shares the 2005 prize, the comb is part of how clocks are read out, and the 2012 Wineland prize was explicitly motivated partly by ion clocks, so a committee could read this as a third prize for the same chain. There is also an argument that it is better to wait for the SI second to be redefined, and that the instrument is a (superb) measurement technique more than a discovery about nature, which is the distinction I normally care about. Finally, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups all have claims that a two-person list leaves out.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as an instrument that changes what can be measured, with a clean Katori-Ye credit and independent confirmation by many laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on the maturity and on the clean credit, and I would add that the case is stronger than 'better instrument' because the clocks are now sensitive to physics, for example the redshift across a single cloud and collective many-body effects. I disagree slightly with leaning on the redefinition of the second: the science stands without it, and the committee should not make the prize depend on a metrology-body decision. I also take his hesitation about Lemonde and Ludlow seriously; I think the citation should be written around the invention (magic-wavelength lattice trapping and its realisation) so that it does not overclaim over the later contributors.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED (B006) first because it is a clean experiment that makes quantum physics controllable and is the architecture of superconducting processors, and notes his own proximity to that community.
responses.response: I respect that argument and I rank B006 highly on originality, but I have three reservations that keep it below B046 for me. First, the 2025 prize has just covered superconducting circuits, and adding another circuit prize this soon leaves little room for other fields. Second, the attribution is harder: four credited names, a three-person cap, and Devoret-school transmon contributions in the background, so any choice is contentious. Third, I would like the committee to judge circuit QED by the physics, such as strong coupling and dispersive readout, rather than by its role in quantum computing. I do not rule it out and would be glad to hear whether Goran thinks the Girvin-or-Blais question can be settled, but given his stated proximity he should weigh whether to step back from that ballot.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the clock second, finds performance verified and reproduced, but asks whether Ye's 2005 prize and the weight of the broader JILA programme, or waiting for the redefinition of the second, count against it.
responses.response: Ye's earlier prize is not a barrier in itself, since the committee has awarded a second prize to different work before, and the lattice clock is a different achievement from the comb. The point I would press is that the citation must be explicit about it. On waiting: I see no benefit, because the independent confirmation is already there and delay only risks more contested credit. I would, however, welcome her view on whether the JILA programme as a whole is better credited through Ye alone or with a third name.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B038) first as a clean theory-to-experiment chain with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi-based materials.
responses.response: I defer to him and to Olsson on condensed matter, and I agree that the Kane-Mele prediction followed by Molenkamp's HgTe observation is exactly the verified chain of discovery that I value. My difficulty is attribution, which he himself raises: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the three-dimensional materials are outside the three names, and Zhang is deceased. If the committee can make a citation around the quantum spin Hall effect that excludes those parts honestly, B038 is a strong alternative; otherwise B046 has the clearer allocation. I also note that the 2016 topological-phases prize makes this a related-field question, much as the 2005 and 2012 prizes do for clocks, so I should apply the same standard to both.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B025) first as a new observational window, with firm detection of the diffuse flux, but concedes that a one-person prize is hard to justify and that the sources are mostly unidentified.
responses.response: I agree that opening a new window is the kind of result the Prize is for, and I would not dismiss it because it is outside my field. My concern is the same as his: a single-name credit for a large collaboration, with AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers in the background, is a weaker allocation than a clock prize with two named inventors, and the source population is still incomplete. I defer to him and to Danielsson on the astroparticle side, but I would ask what a defensible multi-person IceCube citation looks like before ranking it above B046.

uncertainties: Whether a third prize in the same precision-metrology chain (after 2005 and 2012) will be seen by the committee as dilution, and how explicit the citation must be about what is new.

Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow, or the ion-clock groups, have claims strong enough to alter a two-person list; I rely on memory for the priority history and have not checked it against the original 2003 to 2006 papers.
Whether B009 (five credited names, with Zoller and Cirac recurring in other ballots) can be given a fair three-person allocation, which decides whether it is a better alternative than B038.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B046 from my profile: Katori and Ye are not among my listed collaborators, although I work in the same atomic-physics community and have long collaborated with the 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier. I have worked with some groups connected to the ultracold-atom and attosecond fields, so a mild proximity exists to AMO candidates such as B009, which I would flag if the committee moves to them.
